text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure: each token kept in my own account nets me 1 point but costs each of the other three members 0.75 points, while each token placed in the group account earns me 0.75 points with no effect on anyone else's score.

Comparing individually, keeping dominates contributing since 1 beats 0.75 for me personally, making full defection the Nash equilibrium — but that leaves everyone at -25 points versus the much better cooperative outcome of 15 points each if everyone contributed fully. With 10 repeated rounds, I'm considering whether conditional cooperation strategies could sustain the better social outcome.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure of this public goods game, where each member allocates 20 tokens between a private account (worth 1 to self, -0.75 to others) and a group account (worth 0.75 to everyone). I'm setting up variables for tokens kept versus contributed to calculate individual point totals.

Comparing scenarios, keeping all tokens yields more for an individual (1 > 0.75), so defection is the dominant strategy, while full cooperation maximizes collective payoff -- the classic social dilemma tension. I'm calculating specific numbers: if everyone cooperates, each person nets 60 points total, but if one person defects while others cooperate, they can earn even more by free-riding off the group contributions.

Since this spans ten rounds, I think the smarter approach is to start cooperatively in round one to signal good faith, then adapt based on how others behave, similar to a tit-for-tat strategy.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
Each member starts with 20 tokens. Keeping a token privately gives me 1 point but costs each of the other three members 0.75, a total externality of 2.25. Putting it in the group account gives me only 0.75 but has no negative effect on others, so private tokens are socially wasteful compared to group contributions.

If everyone defects and keeps all 20 private, each person ends up at 20 - 45 = -25 points, whereas full cooperation (everyone contributes all 20 to the group) yields 15 points each. Even though keeping tokens private is the individually dominant strategy (1 > 0.75), the mutual cooperation outcome is far better for everyone, so since this is a repeated 10-round game, I'll open with full cooperation and contribute all 20 tokens to signal goodwill and see how the group responds.

I'm working out the payoff structure: each player keeps some tokens privately and contributes the rest to the group fund, where private tokens count fully toward their own score but each token others keep privately costs me points, while the group total gets multiplied and shared back.

Comparing full defection (everyone keeps everything) versus full cooperation (everyone contributes all 20), cooperation yields far higher collective payoffs even though individually keeping a token nets slightly more than contributing it. Since this is a repeated 10-round game, I think starting with full cooperation by contributing all 20 tokens in round one is a reasonable opening move, with room to adjust based on how others respond.
